analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush-era income tax cuts permanent and cuts every income tax rate by 5%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, received no cosponsors, and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the temporary income tax cuts from 2001 and 2003 — lower rates on regular income and lower taxes on dividends and capital gains — and make them permanent, rather than letting them expire. On top of that, it would cut every individual income tax rate by a further 5% (for example, the 25% rate would become 23.75% and the top 35% rate would become 33.25%). It was introduced on the first day of the 112th Congress, sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, and never went anywhere: no hearings, no vote, no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, every income taxpayer would pay slightly less, but the biggest dollar gains would go to high earners and to people who live off investments, since the bill locks in the 2003 law's low tax rates on dividends and capital gains — income that flows mostly to the wealthiest households. The cost would be lower federal revenue, which eventually means more federal debt or cuts elsewhere.

how_it_helps.text: It cuts each individual income tax rate by 5% of its value (for example, the 25% rate becomes 23.75% and the 35% rate becomes 33.25%), which lowers taxes for everyone who owes income tax but saves the most in dollars for those with the highest incomes.
It repeals the scheduled expiration of the 2003 law's reduced tax rates on dividend and capital gain income, permanently locking in lower taxes on investment income.

analysis.who_pays: With no spending cuts or offsets in the bill, the lost federal revenue would be paid for through borrowing and larger deficits, and ultimately by future taxpayers; any eventual cuts to government services would fall on ordinary households.

drawbacks.text: Cutting every tax rate and making dividend and capital gains cuts permanent would reduce federal revenue substantially, and the bill contains no offsetting spending cuts or tax increases, meaning the cost would be added to the deficit.

Because the benefits concentrate in lower rates on high incomes and on investment income, the largest dollar gains would go to the wealthiest households, while any loss of government services or added federal debt falls on everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax cuts would put more money in most taxpayers' pockets, but the largest benefits by far would flow to the highest earners and owners of stocks and other assets, and the reduced revenue would have to be made up through borrowing, future tax increases, or spending cuts. The bill was never debated or scored publicly, and its lack of cosponsors reflected little support even within its own chamber.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved from there, dying quietly at the end of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which is the committee that handles tax legislation, and no further action was ever taken.
It attracted no cosponsors, not even from fellow Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed the tax code through this bill; the existing 2001 and 2003 tax rules continued as they were, and the burden of the highest tax rates was not reduced as the bill would have done.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the tax code stayed as it was

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 112th Congress and became its only supporter of record; no member cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member acted on the bill — its Republican sponsor — and no one else cosponsored, voted on, or opposed it on the record, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill permanently lowers all individual income tax rates and makes the reduced rates on dividends and capital gains permanent, delivering the largest dollar benefits to the highest earners and owners of investments. The cost shows up as reduced federal revenue and added debt borne by everyone.
